newsitem.title: PERU: Peru starts formal talks with Marxist rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru starts formal talks with Marxist rebels.

text.p: The Peruvian government on Thursday began formal negotiations for the first time with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.
They were the highest-level talks since the rebels stormed the residence more than two months ago.

After three rounds of "preliminary" talks with the rebels' second in command, government negotiator Domingo Palermo sat down with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Amaru (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini for nearly 3-1/2 hours at a safe house.

It was the first time Cerpa had left the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence since he led a group of rebels in the raid on Dec. 17. He was driven to the meeting in a Red Cross car accompanied by his second-in-command Rolly Rojas, alias "The Arab."
As the car covered the short distance from the diplomatic compound, the MRTA rebels sang a revolutionary anthem commemorating fallen comrades and shouted defiant slogans.
"On the 65th day of the takeover of the residence, no one gives up, damn it," the rebels shouted in unison.
"What is the objective of this mission?" shouted a rebel through a megaphone. "To free our prisoners," replied others.

The roughly 15 MRTA rebels' demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades has been a bitter sticking point with the government. President Alberto Fujimori insists he will not consider this demand, although he is prepared to let the hostage-takers seek asylum abroad.

In contrast to the pessimism surrounding previous rounds, Roman Catholic Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, one of three guarantors overseeing negotiations, said Thursday's talks were carried out in "a constructive atmosphere."

He added: "We have started to deal with various important issues which require an in-depth analysis." In keeping with the pact of silence by all sides on the details of the meetings, Cipriani did not specify those issues but announced the next talks would be held on Monday.

Fujimori has said the first round of talks with Rojas were "preliminary" and intended to pave the way for "formal" talks with Cerpa to find a bloodless solution to the crisis. In earlier meetings, Rojas and Palermo stated their preliminary positions and agreed to an agenda.
The renewal of direct contact last week after a long period of deadlock and mutual insults prompted speculation the MRTA might shift its position on the prisoners issue.

In an interview with Reuters at a secret jungle location in eastern Peru this week, the MRTA admitted publicly for the first time it probably would not win its central demand that all jailed comrades be freed.

"I do not think all of the 400-plus (prisoners) are going to get out," said a man who identified himself as Comrade Alejandro, a member of the MRTA's top policy-making body. He said the MRTA was prepared to negotiate how many would be freed depending on their experience and importance in the movement.
The jungle commander also doubted Cerpa would ever drop completely the demand for the release of jailed rebels.

Also present at Thursday's talks were the two other guarantors -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent. The Japanese government's observer Terusuke Terada also attended.
A metal detector was used to make sure nobody entered the Red Cross-supervised safe house with weapons.

The MRTA stormed the residence on Dec. 17, initially taking more than 500 cocktail party guests hostage. But it released most in the early days of the crisis, holding only those it considered most valuable.

The remaining captives, many middle-aged and now ailing, include Fujimori's younger brother, two government ministers, top security force and judiciary officials, two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.

The rebels insisted on Thursday that no more hostages would be freed on medical grounds, claiming they could get adequate treatment inside the residence. "Any illness is the product of negotiations dragging on," a statement issued over the Internet on behalf of the MRTA's high command said.

Despite more sophisticated medical attention in the last few weeks, concern for the hostages' health has grown due to increasing signs of stress. Some require close monitoring for cancer, heart problems and arthritis.
The last two hostages released from the compound were freed on medical grounds in January.
